extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, historians, and students of advertising
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical examples for composing and assessing 19th-century handbills, posters, and inscriptions—covering copy, layout, claims, pricing, spectacle, and tactics used to attract and persuade audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed sensory description to persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lavish, tangible detail to make an offering 'utterly irresistible' (e.g., description of the elm coffin 'covered with superfine black... two rows all round, close drove, best black japanned nails', 'handsome crape shroud, cap, and pillow', 'handsome velvet pall').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ visual and tactile imagery to evoke desire or comfort (funeral society ad). This creates emotional pull — effective for services promising dignity/comfort. Beware: excessive ornamentation can seem mawkish or contrived if audience values differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear pricing and payment terms
rubrics_metrics.description: State entrance fees, recurring payments, membership terms and locations for payment (example: 'paying one shilling entrance, and twopence per week... Members to be free in six months. The money to be paid at Mr. Middleton's').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precise fees, schedules, and where/how to pay to reduce friction. Include any conditions (e.g., membership duration). Omitting this invites confusion and reduces conversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Itemized specification of goods/services included
rubrics_metrics.description: List exactly what is supplied (e.g., the funeral notice enumerates coffin type, nails, ornamental drops, inscription plate, handles, pitching, lining, crape, pall, cloaks, hatbands, hood, gloves, porters, attendant, burial fees up to one guinea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An itemized list builds trust and lets buyers compare value. Use specific, measurable descriptions to avoid disputes. Overly vague promises reduce perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to social status and class values
rubrics_metrics.description: Target audience's pride and fears (example: industrious classes 'clubbed their twopences to avoid... the disgrace of a parish funeral'; a labouring man's 'greatest pride... gave wife, parent, or child a good funeral').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align copy with audience values (status, respectability). Framing offerings as avoiding shame or conferring pride can be persuasive. Ethical caution: manipulation of shame can backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shop signs and visual devices for branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ memorable shop signs and devices (e.g., the 'First and Last' sign combining cradle and coffin; exhibition of both cradle and coffin as a device attracting attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive visual branding/signage draws notice in crowded streets. Combine pictorial devices with a memorable motto to strengthen recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ humour, parody, and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use whimsical names, parody, and comic conceits in bills (examples: 'Theatre of Epicurean Variety', character names Signiors Tea Coffee Sugar; burletta 'SOMETHING LIKE BREAKFAST').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour and parody can entertain and increase shareability. Playful devices (punning character names, absurd premises) make bills memorable, but must match audience taste to avoid offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular pricing and separate-ticket options
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer tickets for separate branches of an entertainment with prices and hours specified ('tickets of admission may be had for the separate branches of the entertainment, the price of which together with the hours of performance are specified').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide buyers choice (pick-and-pay) and clear schedules to broaden appeal and lower entry barriers for casual customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage celebrity and performer names
rubrics_metrics.description: Name celebrated performers prominently to attract audiences ('celebrated foreign performers', 'celebrated old Roscius').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach recognized names to signal quality and draw crowds. Ensure claims are truthful; false celebrity association harms credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear schedules and house rules
rubrics_metrics.description: State performance hours, closing time, and on-site arrangements (e.g., 'Hours from 8 to 10 A.M.', 'Theatre closed every Evening at half past Eleven', 'A stout and venerable white-headed Porter... will attend').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical operational details reassure customers and set expectations. Include rules and on-site facilities for comfort and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical spectacle as proof of authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy real, attention-grabbing displays or stunts to prove claims (example: a hairdresser hung a freshly killed bear 'whole in full sight in his shop' and posted 'A fresh bear killed this day!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacles create immediate attention and serve as proof of product authenticity. They are memorable but may be sensational or ethically questionable; consider legal/social acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter competitors' deception with demonstrable evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to rival false claims by inviting inspection or showing processes ('walk in and ''see theirs with their own eyes, cut and weighed from the animal'').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When competitors make dubious claims, provide transparent demonstrations or let customers verify quality themselves to restore trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative endorsements or origin claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim official licensing or notable sourcing to bolster credibility ('Licensed by the Imperial Government — Here, and at Archangel', 'formerd establishment in Russia for catching them wild').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of licensing, government, or reputable origin increase perceived legitimacy. Ensure such claims are accurate to avoid legal/ethical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold hyperbole to create allure (with credibility risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ extravagant description and superlatives to magnify appeal (Robins's 'Cyclopean structure... the Dome, the vast and wondrous Dome'), but risk overstatement (the Colosseum was 'one of the greatest failures').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole can attract attention and create expectations, but if reality falls short it damages reputation. Balance vivid promotion with truthful deliverables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandiose literary language and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use poetic, elevated language and comparisons to famous landmarks or art to confer prestige ('Its mighty graduations', 'Vies in air with earth's chief structures', comparisons to St. Paul's and Versailles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary flourishes can elevate perceived value for culturally literate audiences. Avoid pretension when targeting pragmatic or price-sensitive customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use attendance figures and social proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicize visitor numbers or paid admissions as evidence of success ('Two Thousand Eight Hundred Persons HAVE PAID FOR ADMISSION DURING ONE DAY').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social proof persuades by indicating popularity. Use accurate figures and context; inflated numbers undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote financial returns or profitability claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertise earnings or revenue potential to entice investors/partners ('Three to Five Thousand Pounds a Year').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial claims attract investors but must be substantiated. Unsupported income claims are risky and may be deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refresh offerings to sustain audience interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage frequent changes or new attractions ('continued success will be rendered certain by a change of scene', 'magic influence of Stanfield's pencil to create a new sensation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly updating exhibits or programming retains repeat visitors and generates new publicity. Plan logistics and marketing for changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative prestige and cultural references
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the offering with celebrated buildings, paintings, or artists to transfer prestige (references to St. Paul's, the 'Fountains of Versailles', Stanfield's pencil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic comparisons can elevate status by association. Be mindful of audience recognition and avoid misleading equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive product listing and value claims
rubrics_metrics.description: List an extensive range of goods and emphasize quality and low prices (John Catcheside's verse enumerates teas, sugars, coffees, cocoa, tobacco, spices, oils, dyes, salts, etc., and claims 'I do sell at a low rate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad, explicit inventory reassures customers that you serve many needs; pairing with price/value claims increases persuasion. Over-long lists can fatigue readers—use formatting/organization when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of verse and poetry as an advertising device
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose ads in verse or rhyme to attract attention and charm local audiences (examples: John Catcheside's long rhymed grocery advertisement; the fortune-teller's rhymed invocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic form can aid memorability and local flavor. Ensure readability; poor verse may seem amateurish and reduce authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimic official documents or proclamations for visual hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Format a bill to resemble government proclamations or formal notices to capture attention (example: a bill beginning 'PROCLAMATION' and phrased in royal style for a Hoxton entertainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Styling as official copy can create immediate notice and lend implied gravitas. Avoid impersonating actual government communications to prevent legal/ethical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: State event purpose, beneficiary, and key particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit the event's purpose (charity/benefit), beneficiaries, featured acts, and distinguishing features ('for the Benefit of Himself', listing Miss Phillips, Prince of Wales appearance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conveying the cause or beneficiary helps motivate attendance. Include who benefits and notable participants to increase legitimacy and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear call-to-action and ticketing instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Give precise instructions for applying or obtaining tickets (e.g., 'All applications to be made (for Tickets) on or before ASH WEDNESDAY... At the office Royal Britannia Saloon, Hoxton Old Town').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct CTA and explicit process reduces friction. Provide deadlines, locations, and any payment or reservation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunistic topical marketing (including exploitative framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie promotions to current events or public incidents (example: a linen-draper printed a large mourning-bordered handbill referencing the Overend and Gurney failure to market goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical hooks can amplify relevance and reach. Ethical considerations: exploiting tragedies may alienate audiences; weigh reputational risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison pricing / use of two sets of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Present two price lists—market prices and offered prices—to highlight discounts (noted practice: making up two sets of figures on goods had been found efficacious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison pricing makes savings salient. Use honest, verifiable comparisons; fabricated 'was' prices are deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit contributors to demonstrate professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: List contributors and production credits (e.g., 'Guards, Messrs Cayenne etc. Scenery by Messrs Diaper and Assistants. Dresses by Mrs Cook. Music... by Messrs Knife and Fork').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributing contributors signals organization and quality, and can attract fans of named artisans. Helps establish trust for larger productions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic emphasis and exclamatory signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitalization, exclamation, and typographic prominence for impact ('GOD SAVE THE QUEEN!!!', headings in capitals like 'PROCLAMATION', 'THE COLOSSEUM'S GRANDEUR').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typographic emphasis grabs attention in display copy. Use intentionally—overuse reduces impact and can appear noisy or inexpert.
